title: A family can count as a participating taxpayer while some eligible credit dollars remain unclaimed
source_unit: Census/IRS CES-26-49 Exact Match estimates linking the 2022 CPS ASEC to IRS administrative tax and advance-payment records for tax year 2021
geography: United States; national estimates for eligible tax units/taxpayers and eligible CTC/ACTC dollars

denominator.unit: study-defined eligible taxpayer denominator and separate modeled eligible CTC/ACTC dollar denominator

taxpayer_participation.unit: share of eligible taxpayers who received a CTC/ACTC payment

dollar_participation.unit: share of modeled eligible CTC/ACTC dollars paid

eligible_nonparticipants.value: approximately 3.1 million taxpayers, or 9% of eligible taxpayers
eligible_nonparticipants.unit: eligible taxpayers who did not participate

unclaimed_dollars.value: approximately $26 billion, including $6.9 billion among non-filers, $5.9 billion among filers claiming no CTC/ACTC, and $13.2 billion among under-claimants
unclaimed_dollars.unit: estimated eligible dollars not paid or not fully claimed

nonparticipant_composition.value: 82% of eligible nonparticipants were in tax units with adjusted gross income below $75,000; 53% filed a return

observations.method: The study uses CPS ASEC survey information to model tax units, qualifying dependents, eligibility, and eligible credit amounts with NBER TAXSIM, then links people to IRS administrative tax and advance-payment records using protected identifiers. IRS records identify claimed and paid amounts; survey weights are adjusted for linked-person coverage.
observations.uncertainty: The estimates are conditional on modeled eligibility and are subject to error in tax-unit and dependent modeling, survey-to-tax reference-period differences, income differences, population-concept differences, probabilistic linkage, and survey nonresponse/imputation. The authors note the 2021 estimates use a new methodology and may be revised, especially unclaimed-dollar estimates.
observations.subgroup: National eligible taxpayer and dollar estimates, with reported comparisons by household head sex, marital status, number of qualifying dependents, income, filing status, and nonparticipant composition. These are tax-unit and dollar groups, not a longitudinal household panel.
observations.counterinterpretation: The gap between taxpayer and dollar participation may reflect under-claiming among people with different modeled credit amounts, eligibility-model error, non-filing, household/tax-unit differences, or timing and advance-payment reconciliation rather than one single administrative barrier. High participation does not prove adequate benefit size, timely receipt, or improved household security.

related_sources.claim: The 2020 CTC/ACTC paper uses a prior methodology and is a related year, not the same estimate; the 2021 paper says the methods are not directly comparable.

boundary: This record adds a benefit-eligibility-to-payment conversion boundary. It does not establish why an eligible taxpayer did not claim or receive a dollar, whether the credit arrived on time, what households spent it on, whether it was adequate, or whether it changed durable poverty, health, care, trust, or political action.
